drafts.title: $4.7 million almost went to a fake Elon
drafts.angle: Tesla fans were the target. A fake Elon on a fake livestream. Nobody got hacked; people sent the money themselves. Protect-your-parents save.
bullets: During Tesla's flying car demo, scammers ran a fake YouTube livestream with a deepfake Elon promising to double any crypto sent.
500,000+ people watched; hundreds of Coinbase customers tried to send millions in about two hours.
Coinbase says its AI scam defenses stopped about 91%, $4.7 million, automatically (Coinbase blog, Nov 17).
No passwords stolen, no accounts broken into. The scam worked on trust.
drafts.body: $4.7 million almost went to a fake Elon. Deepfake livestream, fake Tesla giveaway, send crypto and get double back. 500,000 people watched. My rule: {my one rule for anything that promises to double money}. Would your parents spot this one?
drafts.framework_body:
$4.7 million almost went to a fake Elon.

During Tesla's big demo, scammers ran their own YouTube livestream. It looked real. It sounded real. It was an AI copy of Elon telling people to send crypto and he'd send double back.

More than 500,000 people watched it. Hundreds of people tried to send money in about two hours.

Coinbase says its own AI caught about 91% of it and stopped $4.7 million before it left. Good for them. But think about the other 9%.

Here's the part that matters: nobody got hacked. No passwords stolen. People pushed the button themselves because they trusted the face on the screen.

So here's what I'm telling {an older family member or friend} this week:
1. Elon is not giving away money. Nobody is.
2. Anything that says send money first, get double back, is a scam. Every time.
3. {my one rule for anything that promises to double money}.

AI can fake a face and a voice now. It can't fake common sense.

Would your parents spot this one?

drafts.pixel: Face to camera: "Elon is never giving away crypto. Here's how I'd explain this to {an older family member or friend}."

drafts.title: $0 to have AI sit on hold for you
drafts.angle: The sit-on-hold job just got handed to AI, free on your phone. Practical time saver, no jargon.
bullets: Google made Gemini Tasks free on Nov 17 in the US, Canada, Japan, Korea, Australia and India; no paid plan needed.
Google's example: Gemini called the two nearest dealerships for a service appointment, checked the calendar and booked it in under five minutes.
Google says Gemini tells the business up front that it's an AI.
WSJ's Joanna Stern joked that Google already has an app called Google Tasks.

drafts.framework_body:
$0 to have AI sit on hold for you now.

Google just made this free on your phone. You tell Gemini what you need, like a service appointment, and it calls the places for you. It finds an open time and puts it on your calendar.

Google's own example: it called the two closest dealerships, checked the calendar and booked the appointment in under five minutes. And it tells the business right away that it's an AI, so nobody's being tricked.

This is the kind of AI I want people to know about. Not robots. Not scary headlines. Just getting back the 40 minutes you spend listening to hold music.
